sentences.text: Timimus hermani was a small theropod dinosaur that lived in Australia during the Early Cretaceous, with a holotype femur measuring 44 centimeters in length and a total estimated length of 2.5 meters.

The genus name Timimus means 'Tim's Mimic', combining the names of the discoverers' son Timothy Rich and paleontologist Tim Flannery, while the species name hermani honors the volunteer John Herman who assisted the Dinosaur Cove project.
A fossilized toe bone from a possible Timimus relative shows a depressed fracture on the bottom surface, suggesting injury.
A 2016 estimate suggests the holotype specimen was 4.3 meters long and weighed 200 kilograms.
Two femurs, one from an adult and one from a juvenile, were discovered within one meter of each other at the Dinosaur Cove East site in southern Australia in 1991.
Timimus hermani was formally named and described by Dr. Thomas Rich and Patricia Vickers-Rich in 1993 or 1994.
The holotype specimen dates to the Albian stage of the Early Cretaceous, approximately 106 million years ago.
Timimus lived in polar forests with mild summers and cold, dark winters due to the region's proximity to the South Pole in the Early Cretaceous.

Analysis of bone microstructure suggests Timimus may have hibernated during colder months, unlike the ornithischian Leaellynasaura, as indicated by cyclical bone growth patterns in Timimus suggesting it hibernated during the cold nights of the Early Cretaceous.

Timimus was originally classified as an ornithomimosaur but is now thought to be a tyrannosauroid, as it lacks shared derived traits with ornithomimosaurs, providing no proof of its membership in that group.

A 2010 study classified Timimus within Paraves, possibly as an indeterminate dromaeosaurid related to Unenlagiinae, while a 2012 study identified Timimus as a valid tyrannosauroid, a view supported by later analyses that placed it either within Tyrannosauroidea or as a sister taxon to Tyrannoraptora.
Timimus lived during the Early Cretaceous period, specifically from the Albian to the Cenomanian stages, between 113.2 and 93.9 million years ago.
